title: The Canterville Ghost
author: Oscar Wilde
ru: Американская семья покупает английский замок с привидением — и привидению становится страшнее, чем им

chapters.title: Chapter 1. A House with a Ghost
chapters.text:
Mr Hiram B. Otis was an important American. He worked for his country in London, and he wanted to buy a fine old English house. He chose Canterville Chase, and he went to see the owner, Lord Canterville.

Lord Canterville was an honest man.

“There is a ghost in the house,” he said. “My family saw it many times. One evening my great-aunt was dressing for dinner, and she felt two skeleton hands on her shoulders. She was never well again after that.”

“My Lord,” said Mr Otis, “I come from a modern country. We have everything money can buy. If there was a real ghost in Europe, some clever American would buy it and put it in a museum.”

“I'm afraid the ghost is real,” said Lord Canterville sadly. “It always appears before a death in our family.”

“Well, so does the family doctor,” answered Mr Otis. “There's no such thing as a ghost, sir. And the laws of Nature won't change for English lords.”

So Mr Otis bought the house, the furniture and the ghost.

The Otis family was a large one. Mrs Otis was a handsome woman, and in many ways she was very English. This shows that the English and the Americans have everything in common today — except, of course, language. Their eldest son, Washington, was famous in London for one thing: he danced better than anyone. Next came Virginia. She was fifteen, small and lovely, with big blue eyes, and she rode a horse better than most men. The two youngest were twin boys. They were never still and never quiet, so everybody called them “the Stars and Stripes”.

The family arrived at Canterville Chase on a lovely July evening. But as they came near the house, the sky suddenly went dark, and a strange silence filled the air.

Mrs Umney, the old housekeeper, was waiting at the door in a black dress and a white cap. She took them into the library for tea. There, on the floor by the fireplace, Mrs Otis saw a dark red stain.

“Oh dear,” she said. “Somebody spilled something.”

“Yes, madam,” said Mrs Umney quietly. “Blood was spilled there. Lady Eleanore de Canterville was killed on that very spot by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Nine years later, Sir Simon disappeared, and nobody ever found his body. His ghost still walks in this house, and the blood stain cannot be removed.”

“That's nonsense,” cried Washington. He took a little black stick out of his pocket. “Pinkerton's Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it in a second!”

He went down on his knees and rubbed the floor hard. A few seconds later, the stain was gone.

Suddenly there was a terrible flash of lightning and a great crash of thunder. Mrs Umney screamed and fainted.

“What a terrible climate!” said Mr Otis calmly. “I think England has too many people and not enough good weather for all of them.”

“My dear Hiram,” said Mrs Otis, “what can we do with a woman who faints?”

“Take it out of her pay, like broken plates,” said Mr Otis. “She won't faint after that.”

And in a few moments, Mrs Umney opened her eyes.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Stain That Came Back
chapters.text:
Mrs Umney sat up and looked at the family with frightened eyes.

“Be careful,” she said. “I saw things in this house with my own eyes, sir. Things that will make your hair stand on end.”

Mr and Mrs Otis told her kindly that they were not afraid of ghosts. Then the old housekeeper asked for more money and went to bed.

Nothing else happened that night. But the next morning, the family came down to breakfast and found the terrible red stain on the library floor again.

“It isn't the fault of the Paragon Detergent,” said Washington. “I use it on everything. It must be the ghost.”

He cleaned the stain away a second time. But the next morning it was back. And the morning after that, too.

So one night Mr Otis locked the library door himself and put the key in his pocket. In the morning the door was still locked, but the stain was there again.

Now the family was really interested. Mr Otis began to think that perhaps he was wrong about ghosts. Mrs Otis wanted to join a society for the study of ghosts. And Washington wrote a long letter to Pinkerton's about the stain.

That night they got their answer.

At one o'clock, Mr Otis woke up. He could hear a strange noise in the corridor outside his room. Clank, clank, clank. It sounded like metal, and it was coming nearer. Mr Otis got up, put on his slippers, took a small bottle from his bag, and opened the door.

There, in the pale moonlight, stood an old man. His eyes were red like burning coals. His long grey hair fell over his shoulders, and his old-fashioned clothes were dirty and torn. Heavy chains hung from his wrists and his ankles.

“My dear sir,” said Mr Otis politely, “I really must ask you to oil those chains. They are very noisy, and people are trying to sleep. I have brought you a bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. One use is enough. I'll leave it here for you, next to the candles. And if you need more, just ask.”

Then Mr Otis put the bottle on a little table, went back into his bedroom and closed the door.

For a moment the Canterville ghost stood still. He was too angry to move. Then he threw the bottle on the floor, ran down the corridor and filled the air with terrible green light and horrible groans.

But just then, a door opened. Two small figures in white nightshirts appeared, and a big pillow flew past his head!

The ghost quickly disappeared through the wall.

In his secret room, the ghost sat down in the moonlight and tried to calm down. He had never been so insulted in three hundred years! He thought of his great successes. There were the four housemaids who screamed for a week after he smiled at them through the curtains. There was the old lady who woke up and found a skeleton in her armchair, reading her diary.

And now these terrible modern Americans offered him oil for his chains and threw pillows at his head!

“They will pay for this,” he said.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Sir Simon Fights Back
chapters.text:
The next day, the family talked about the ghost at breakfast.

“I don't want to be rude to him,” said Mr Otis. “But he didn't take my present. That was not polite. And if he won't use the Rising Sun Lubricator, we'll have to take his chains away.”

For a week, nobody saw the ghost. But every morning the blood stain was on the library floor again. And something very strange was happening to it. One morning it was dark red, the next morning bright red, then purple. And one morning, when the family came down to pray before breakfast, it was bright green!

The family thought this was great fun. Every evening they made bets about the colour of tomorrow's stain. Only Virginia did not join the game. The stain always made her a little sad, and on the morning of the green stain she almost cried.

The ghost's second visit was on Sunday night. Soon after the family went to bed, a terrible crash came from the hall. Everyone ran downstairs. An old suit of armour was lying on the stone floor, and the Canterville ghost was sitting in a big old chair next to it, rubbing his knees. He wanted to frighten the family in the armour, so he tried to put it on. But it was much too heavy for him now, and he fell over with a crash.

The twins had their pea-shooters with them, and they began to shoot little dry peas at him. Mr Otis pointed his gun at him.

“Hands up!” he said.

The ghost jumped up with a wild cry. He flew through them like a cold mist, and as he went, he blew out Washington's candle. At the top of the stairs, he stopped and laughed his famous laugh. Once, long ago, this laugh turned Lord Raker's hair grey in a single night.

Then a bedroom door opened, and Mrs Otis came out in her light blue dressing gown.

“I'm afraid you're not well,” she said kindly. “I brought you a bottle of Doctor Dobell's medicine. If your stomach hurts, it will help.”

The ghost looked at her angrily. He decided to change into a big black dog. But just then he heard the twins running up the stairs. So he only gave a weak little groan and disappeared.

For several days after that, the ghost stayed in his room. The Americans were rude and stupid, he thought. But he was a Canterville, and a Canterville never gives up!

So he made a plan for Friday, the seventeenth of August. First he would visit Washington, who always cleaned away the stain, and whisper terrible words into his ear. Then he would visit the twins. He would sit on their chests until they could not breathe, and then stand between their beds as a green, ice-cold dead body until they screamed and screamed.

He chose his clothes carefully. He was going to be “Red Reuben, the Terrible Murderer” — one of his greatest parts.

On Friday night, at a quarter past eleven, the family went to bed. The ghost waited for the clock to strike midnight. Then he picked up his old knife and stepped quietly into the corridor.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Other Ghost
chapters.text:
It was a wild night. The wind was shaking the windows, and the rain was falling hard. The ghost smiled. It was perfect weather for a murderer.

He moved through the house like a shadow. Washington's room was near now. In a few minutes, that stupid young man with his Paragon Detergent would learn some respect!

He turned the corner of the corridor. And then he stopped.

In front of him stood something terrible.

It was very tall and white. Its head was round and bald, and its fat white face had a horrible wide smile. Red fire burned in its eyes. Its body was covered with a long white cloth, and in one hand it was holding a big, shining knife. On its chest there was a piece of paper with some old-fashioned writing.

The Canterville ghost had never seen a ghost before. He gave a high scream, like a little girl, and ran. He ran all the way back to his room, jumped into bed and pulled the sheets over his head.

For a long time he lay there, shaking. But slowly he began to feel braver.

“I am a Canterville,” he thought. “And two ghosts are better than one. When the sun comes up, I will go and talk to my new friend. Together we will frighten those twins until they cry for their mother!”

Early in the morning, he went back to the corridor. The other ghost was still there. But something was wrong with it. The light in its eyes was gone. The knife was lying on the floor. And it was leaning against the wall in a very strange way.

He took it in his arms. To his horror, the head fell off and rolled across the floor. The white cloth fell down, and he found himself holding a broom, a kitchen knife and an old white bedsheet. The terrible head was only a big hollow turnip with a candle inside!

Now he could read the paper on its chest:

THE OTIS GHOST.
THE ONLY REAL AND ORIGINAL GHOST.
BEWARE OF CHEAP COPIES!

He understood everything. It was a trick. Those terrible twins!

The ghost shook his thin old hands in the air. He made a great promise in the old style of his family.

“When the cock crows twice,” he cried, “there will be blood! Death will walk silently through this house!”

As he finished, a cock crowed somewhere far away on a farm — its loud morning cry. The ghost laughed his long, horrible laugh and waited for the second cry.

He waited and waited. The cock did not crow again.

At half past seven, the housemaids arrived, and the ghost had to go back to his room. There he took down his favourite old books and read them carefully. In every story, the cock always crowed twice. Always!

“The cock is American too,” he thought bitterly. “There is no other explanation.”

For five days, he did not leave his room. He was too tired, too ill and too unhappy. And at the end of those five days, he made a big decision. The family did not want the blood stain? Very well. They could live without it.

He never painted the stain on the library floor again.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Bad Nights for Sir Simon
chapters.text:
But a ghost has his duties. Every first and third Wednesday of the month, he had to appear at the big window. On every second and fourth Friday, he had to groan in the corridors at midnight. Sir Simon took his work seriously, so he continued to walk through the house at night.

But he was careful now. He took off his heavy boots and walked very softly over the old wooden floors. And he oiled his chains with the Rising Sun Lubricator. He hated to do it, but it was true — the American oil really worked. Now his chains made no noise at all.

It was no use. The twins were always waiting for him.

One night they put a string across the dark corridor, and he fell over it. Another night they put butter on the top step of the stairs. He was going down in a hurry, and he slipped and fell all the way to the bottom. Every part of his old body hurt.

This was too much. He decided to try one last great part: “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl”. Seventy years before, a beautiful young lady saw him as the Headless Earl, and she refused to marry Lord Canterville's grandfather. She ran away with handsome young Jack Castleton instead, because she would never marry into a family with such a horrible ghost.

It took him three full hours to get ready. At a quarter past one in the morning, he walked to the twins' bedroom. The door was a little open. He pushed it hard, with a terrible cry.

A big jug of cold water fell on him from the top of the door. He was wet to the skin. From the beds came loud screams — screams of laughter.

He ran back to his room. The next day, he was in bed with a very bad cold. There was only one good thing about that night: he did not have his head with him, so at least his head stayed dry.

After that, he stopped trying to frighten the twins. He walked around the house in soft slippers, with a thick red scarf around his neck. And he carried a little gun, in case the twins attacked.

But they found him anyway. One night, in a dark corridor, the twins jumped out at him. They waved their arms and shouted “BOO!” into his ear.

The poor ghost was terribly frightened. He ran for the staircase, but Washington was waiting there with a big garden sprayer full of water. So the ghost had to escape into the cold, empty fireplace and climb up the chimney. He arrived back in his room black with dirt and completely miserable.

After that night, nobody saw him. Every night the twins put nutshells in the corridors to make him trip, but the ghost did not come out.

Mr Otis went back to his great book about the history of the American Democratic Party. Mrs Otis organised a clambake — a big American seafood party — and the neighbours talked about it for weeks. The boys played noisy American games, and Virginia rode her pony around the park with the young Duke of Cheshire.

Everybody agreed. The ghost was gone.

They were wrong.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. A Very Tired Ghost
chapters.text:
The ghost was still in the house. He was just too tired to come out.

The young Duke of Cheshire was spending the last week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. Fifty years before, the ghost had played dice with the Duke's great-uncle and frightened him so badly that the poor man could only say two words for the rest of his life: “Double sixes!” Now the ghost wanted to visit the young Duke as “The Vampire Monk”. But in the end he was too afraid of the twins. He stayed in his room, and the little Duke slept happily all night and dreamed of Virginia.

A few days later, Virginia tore her dress while she was out riding. She did not want anyone to see her, so she ran up the back stairs. As she passed the Tapestry Chamber, she looked through the open door.

There was the Canterville ghost! He was sitting by the window and watching the golden leaves fly through the air. He was resting his head on his hand, and he looked so lonely and tired that Virginia forgot to be afraid.

“I'm so sorry for you,” she said. “My brothers are going back to school tomorrow. Then, if you behave yourself, nobody will annoy you.”

“Behave myself?” said the ghost. “I must rattle my chains and groan through keyholes and walk around at night. It's the only reason I exist.”

“It's no reason at all,” said Virginia. “And you were very wicked. You killed your wife.”

“Yes, I did,” said the ghost. “But that was a family matter. My wife was very plain. She never ironed my collars properly, and she knew nothing about cooking. And then her brothers locked me up and starved me to death.”

“Starved you to death?” said Virginia. “Oh, Sir Simon, are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my bag. Would you like it?”

“No, thank you. I never eat anything now. But you are very kind — much nicer than the rest of your horrible, rude, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” cried Virginia, and she stamped her foot. “You're the rude one! And you stole the paints out of my box for your silly blood stain. And who ever heard of green blood?”

“Well, what could I do?” said the ghost. “It is very difficult to get real blood these days. And the colour is a question of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, the bluest in England. But I know you Americans don't care about things like that.”

“You should go to America,” said Virginia. “Lots of people in New York would pay a hundred thousand dollars for a grandfather. They would pay much more for a family ghost.”

“I don't think I would like America.”

“Because it has no ruins and no interesting old things?” asked Virginia with a little smile.

“No ruins? No interesting old things?” said the ghost. “You have your navy. And your manners.”

“Good evening,” said Virginia coldly. “I'll ask Papa to give the twins an extra week's holiday.”

“Please don't go, Miss Virginia!” cried the ghost. “I'm so lonely and so unhappy. I want to go to sleep, and I can't.”

“That's silly,” said Virginia. “You just go to bed and blow out the candle. Even babies know how to sleep.”

The ghost looked at her sadly.

“I haven't slept for three hundred years,” he said.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. The Garden of Death
chapters.text:
Virginia came back, knelt down next to the old ghost and looked up into his tired face.

“Poor, poor ghost,” she said softly. “Is there no place where you can sleep?”

“Far away, beyond the pine woods,” he answered in a low, dreamy voice, “there is a little garden. The grass is long and deep there, and a nightingale sings all night long. The cold moon looks down, and the old yew tree spreads its arms over the sleepers.”

Virginia's eyes filled with tears, and she hid her face in her hands.

“You mean the Garden of Death,” she whispered.

“Yes, Death. Death must be so beautiful,” said the ghost. “To lie in the soft brown earth, with the grass above your head, and listen to the silence. To have no yesterday and no tomorrow. To forget time and to forgive life, and to be at peace. You can help me, Virginia. You can open the door of Death's house for me. Love is always with you, and Love is stronger than Death.”

Virginia felt cold and said nothing. Then the ghost spoke again.

“Did you ever read the old words on the library window?”

“Oh, often,” said Virginia. “But I don't know what they mean.” And she said the six strange lines slowly:

When a golden girl can win
A prayer from the lips of sin,
When the dead almond tree has flowers,
And a little child gives away its tears,
Then all the house will be still,
And peace will come to Canterville.

“They mean,” said the ghost, “that you must cry with me for my sins, because I have no tears. And you must pray with me for my soul, because I have no faith. And then, because you are so good and kind, the Angel of Death will have pity on me. You will see terrible shapes in the darkness and hear wicked voices, but they cannot hurt a good child.”

Virginia did not answer, and the ghost looked down at her golden head without hope.

Suddenly she stood up. Her face was pale, but her eyes were shining.

“I am not afraid,” she said firmly. “I will ask the Angel to have pity on you.”

The ghost stood up with a little cry of joy. He took her hand and kissed it. His fingers were as cold as ice, and his lips burned like fire. He led her across the dark room.

As they passed the old tapestry, the little hunters in it began to move and wave their arms.

“Go back, little Virginia!” they cried. “Go back!”

But the ghost held her hand more tightly, and she closed her eyes. Horrible animals with lizard eyes looked at her from the carved fireplace and whispered, “Be careful, little Virginia! We may never see you again!”

At the end of the room, the ghost stopped and said some strange words. She opened her eyes. The wall was slowly disappearing like a mist, and there was a great black hole in front of her. A cold wind blew around them, and something pulled at her dress.

“Quick, quick,” cried the ghost, “or it will be too late!”

And in a moment the wall closed behind them. The Tapestry Chamber was empty.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Where Is Virginia?
chapters.text:
Ten minutes later, the bell rang for tea, but Virginia did not come down. A servant looked for her everywhere and couldn't find her.

At first Mrs Otis was not worried. Virginia often went into the garden to pick flowers for the dinner table. But six o'clock came, and then seven, and still there was no Virginia.

The whole family searched the house from top to bottom. The boys ran around the gardens and called her name. Then Mr Otis remembered the gypsies. A few days earlier, he had kindly allowed them to camp in the park. Perhaps they took his daughter?

He hurried to their camp with Washington and the young Duke, who was almost mad with worry. But the gypsies were gone.

Mr Otis sent messages to the police and rode to the railway station to ask about her. The little Duke followed him on his pony.

“I'm sorry, Mr Otis,” he said, “but I can't go home until we find Virginia. Last year I asked you if I could marry her, and you said we were too young. Now look what happened!”

Mr Otis could not help smiling at the handsome young boy. “Well, Cecil,” he said, “if you won't go back, you must come with me.”

But there was no news of Virginia anywhere. Late at night they rode home, tired and unhappy. The police found the gypsies, but they knew nothing about the little girl.

Nobody wanted any dinner. Even the twins were quiet and sad, because they loved their sister very much. Just before midnight, Mr Otis sent everybody to bed.

They were going up the stairs when the clock struck twelve. Suddenly there was a crash and a terrible cry. A great clap of thunder shook the house, and strange, beautiful music filled the air. A secret door in the wall at the top of the stairs flew open.

And there stood Virginia! She was very pale, and she was holding a little box in her hands.

Everybody ran up to her. Mrs Otis held her tightly. The Duke covered her face with kisses. The twins danced around her like wild animals.

“My dear, where were you?” said Mr Otis angrily. He thought it was a silly joke. “Never play tricks like that again!”

“Except on the ghost!” cried the twins.

“Papa,” said Virginia quietly, “I was with the ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He was very wicked, but he was really sorry for everything he did. Before he died, he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

Washington took a candle, and she led them through the secret door and down a narrow passage to a heavy old door. Virginia touched it, and it opened. Inside was a little low room with one small window.

A skeleton was chained to an iron ring in the wall. It was lying on the stone floor, and its long thin fingers were reaching for an old plate and a jug of water. They were just a little too far away.

Virginia knelt down and began to pray.

Suddenly one of the twins looked out of the window.

“Look!” he cried. “The old dead almond tree in the garden is covered with flowers!”

Virginia stood up. Her face was full of light.

“God has forgiven him,” she said.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. Peace at Canterville
chapters.text:
Four days later, there was a funeral at Canterville Chase. It began at eleven o'clock at night. Eight black horses pulled the funeral carriage slowly through the dark park. Lord Canterville came all the way from Wales for the funeral, and he walked first, next to little Virginia. Behind them came the whole family and the servants.

They buried Sir Simon in a corner of the churchyard, under the old yew tree. Virginia put a beautiful cross of white and pink almond flowers on the grave. At that moment, the moon came out and filled the churchyard with silver light. Far away in a little wood, a nightingale began to sing. Virginia thought of the ghost's words about the Garden of Death, and her eyes filled with tears. She hardly spoke on the way home.

From that night, Canterville Chase was quiet. There were no more chains in the corridors, no groans at midnight and no red stain on the library floor. Peace had come to Canterville at last.

The next morning, before Lord Canterville went back to London, Mr Otis spoke to him about the jewels. They were wonderful, especially a necklace of rubies.

“My Lord,” said Mr Otis, “these jewels belong to your family. I must ask you to take them. We Americans believe in simple living, and these expensive old things are not right for a good republican girl. But she would like to keep the box, if you agree.”

Lord Canterville listened politely and pulled at his grey moustache once or twice.

“My dear sir,” he said at last, “your charming little daughter did my unlucky ancestor, Sir Simon, a very great service. The jewels are hers. And remember — you bought the furniture and the ghost together. So everything that belonged to the ghost is now yours.”

Mr Otis was not happy about it, but he had to agree.

Years later, Virginia married the young Duke of Cheshire. On the day she met the Queen as the new Duchess, she wore the Canterville jewels, and everybody admired her. Even Mr Otis was proud of her. He still did not like dukes very much, as a matter of principle. But he liked his new son-in-law very much indeed.

After the wedding, the Duke and Duchess came to Canterville Chase. One afternoon they walked to the little churchyard under the pine trees. On the stone over the grave were Sir Simon's initials and the six lines from the library window. Virginia put some roses on it. Then the Duke took her hand.

“Virginia,” he said, “a wife should have no secrets from her husband.”

“Dear Cecil, I have no secrets from you.”

“Yes, you do,” he answered with a smile. “You never told me what happened when you were locked up with the ghost.”

“I never told anyone,” said Virginia seriously. “Please don't ask me, Cecil. I can't tell you. Poor Sir Simon! I owe him a lot. Don't laugh, Cecil — I really do. He made me see what Life is, and what Death means, and why Love is stronger than both.”

The Duke kissed his wife lovingly.

“You can have your secret,” he said, “if I can have your heart.”

“You always had my heart, Cecil.”

“And you will tell our children one day, won't you?”

Virginia went pink.
